title: At the Pharisee's Table: Humility, the Great Banquet, and the Cost
summary: At a Sabbath meal in a leading Pharisee's house, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, then teaches the guests to take the lowest seat and the host to invite the poor, who cannot repay. When a guest speaks of the feast in the kingdom of God, Jesus tells of a great banquet whose invited guests make excuses, so the host fills his house with the poor and the outcasts. To the crowds traveling with him he says that discipleship means putting him above family and life itself, and counting the cost.
story:
Jesus has just lamented over Jerusalem and spoken of people coming from every direction to recline at table in God's kingdom (13:29). Now he reclines at a real table, and the meal becomes a picture of that coming feast. Who sits where, who gets invited, and who refuses to come are the questions that decide who will share the kingdom's banquet. This is the third time Luke has Jesus eat in a Pharisee's house (7:36-50, 11:37-54), and the third Sabbath healing that provokes objection (6:6-11, 13:10-17).

Then Luke turns from the dinner party to the road, where large crowds are traveling with Jesus toward Jerusalem, and Jesus makes sure they understand where the road leads: to a cross. The chapter joins the generosity of God's invitation with the seriousness of the response it calls for. Chapter 15 follows with the complaint that Jesus eats with sinners and with his three parables of the lost, which defend the very table fellowship this chapter describes.
historical:
Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to the careful keeping of the Law as interpreted by the traditions of the elders; Josephus describes them as influential with the people (Antiquities 18.12-15). Luke calls the host ‘one of the rulers of the Pharisees’ (verse 1), a leading member, and the meal is on the Sabbath, when the main meal followed the synagogue service and food had been prepared the day before. The ‘experts in the law’ (nomikoi, verse 3) were scribes, specialists in interpreting the Law, and Luke often pairs them with the Pharisees (7:30, 11:45-52). Their silence (verse 4) and inability to answer (verse 6) are a public defeat in an honor culture.

Sabbath rules for rescue varied between Jewish groups. The Damascus Document from Qumran forbids lifting an animal out of a pit or well on the Sabbath (CD 11:13-14), and editors translate its next lines, about a person who falls into water, in opposite ways. Later rabbinic teaching allowed relieving an animal's suffering, for example by bringing cushions to an animal in a pit (b. Shabbat 128b), and held that danger to human life overrides the Sabbath (m. Yoma 8:6). Jesus' question assumes what his hearers actually did: no one would leave his own son, or even his ox, in a well until the Sabbath ended.

Jewish expectation pictured the age to come as a banquet (Isaiah 25:6-8), and the guest's pious remark in verse 15 draws on that hope. Some Jewish groups expected strict limits on who would sit at that table. The Rule of the Congregation from Qumran (1QSa 2:3-10) bars from the assembly of the last days anyone with a physical defect, the lame, the blind, the deaf, and those with a visible blemish, because holy angels are present, and it goes on to describe the meal at which the Messiah of Israel will sit (1QSa 2:11-22). Jesus' list in verses 13 and 21, the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, reads like a deliberate reversal of such exclusions and of the priestly limits of Leviticus 21:17-23.

The parable of the great banquet has a relative in Matthew 22:1-14, where a king gives a wedding feast for his son and the invited guests refuse and even kill his servants, and the king destroys their city. The Gospel of Thomas, saying 64, has another version, with four invitees whose excuses concern business, a house, a friend's wedding, and a farm, ending with the verdict that buyers and merchants will not enter the places of the Father. Some scholars think Jesus told a similar story on more than one occasion, while others think the evangelists adapted one parable. Joachim Jeremias drew attention to a story in the Jerusalem Talmud (y. Sanhedrin 6:6, 23c; y. Hagigah 2:2, 77d) about a rich tax collector named Bar Ma'yan who held a banquet for the town councillors; when they refused to come, he invited the poor instead. The discipleship sayings have parallels in Matthew 10:37-38 and Mark 8:34, and the salt saying in Matthew 5:13 and Mark 9:49-50. The healing of the man with dropsy, the teaching on seats and guests, and the two cost-counting parables are found only in Luke.

The two short parables in verses 28-32 would have had recent examples. Building projects were a mark of status, and the Herods built on a vast scale. Wars between client kings were real: Herod Antipas's army was destroyed by the Nabatean king Aretas IV around AD 36 (Antiquities 18.113-115), a defeat Josephus says many Jews saw as God's punishment for Antipas's execution of John the Baptist (18.116).
cultural:
Dropsy (hudrōpikos, verse 2) was a swelling of the body with retained fluid, often accompanied by great thirst. Greek and Latin moralists used it as a picture of greed, a craving that drinking only increases; Horace compares the greedy man to a dropsy patient whose thirst grows the more he indulges it (Odes 2.2.13-16). Willi Braun (Feasting and Social Rhetoric in Luke 14, 1995) argued that Luke's audience would have heard the healing as an introduction to the chapter's attack on the thirst for honor and wealth, a reading many commentators find suggestive though the text does not spell it out.

Meals in the ancient Mediterranean expressed and reinforced status. Guests reclined on couches arranged around the table, and the place nearest the host was the place of honor (prōtoklisia, verse 7). Plutarch devotes one of his Table Talks to whether a host should assign places or let guests seat themselves, and his speakers assume that rank must be observed (Table Talk 1.2). Jesus' advice in verses 8-10 applies Proverbs 25:6-7, which says it is better to be told to come up than to be put lower before a noble. A similar teaching appears in Leviticus Rabbah 1:5, where Rabbi Akiva, citing Simeon ben Azzai, advises going down two or three seats until you are told to come up, and adds Hillel's saying that his humbling is his exaltation.

Invitations among the well-off were exchanges of obligation: you invite me, I invite you, and both of us gain honor. The Greek words in verses 12-14 (antikaleō, to invite in return; antapodoma, repayment; antapodidōmi, to repay) spell out that circle, and Jesus' instruction to invite those who cannot repay breaks it. The Old Testament had already commanded that the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow share Israel's festival meals (Deuteronomy 14:28-29, 16:11-14). It was customary to send an invitation in advance and then to send a servant to call guests when the meal was ready, as the king's servants came to bring Haman to Esther's banquet (Esther 6:14). To accept and then refuse at the last minute was a public insult to the host.

The excuses are thin. A buyer inspected a field before purchase, not after, and five yoke of oxen, ten animals, were bought after testing, not before; the purchase marks the second man as a substantial farmer. The third excuse echoes the exemptions from military service for a man with a new house, a new vineyard, or a new wife (Deuteronomy 20:5-7, 24:5), but those released a man from war, not from a meal he had already accepted. ‘Streets and alleys of the city’ (verse 21) were where the poor and disabled lived and begged; ‘highways and hedges’ (verse 23) lay outside the town, where travelers, laborers, and those with no home in it could be found, and many interpreters have seen in them the Gentiles to whom Acts will turn.

Hate in verse 26 reflects a Semitic idiom of preference, in which to love one and ‘hate’ another means to choose one over the other. When Genesis says Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, the next verse calls Leah, literally, ‘hated’ (Genesis 29:30-31); Deuteronomy 21:15-17 speaks of a loved and a ‘hated’ wife; and Malachi 1:2-3, quoted in Romans 9:13, has God love Jacob and hate Esau, speaking of election. Matthew 10:37 gives the same saying in comparative form, loving father or mother more than Jesus. Luke's list includes wife, as does his version of Jesus' promise to those who leave home for the kingdom (18:29). A cross in verse 27 was not a metaphor for ordinary troubles: condemned men carried the crossbeam to the place of execution, and after the uprising that followed Herod the Great's death in 4 BC the Roman governor Varus crucified two thousand rebels around Jerusalem (Antiquities 17.295).

Salt was used to season and preserve food and, in small amounts, on soil and manure. Pure sodium chloride does not lose its taste, but salt gathered from the Dead Sea region was mixed with other minerals, and when the salt leached out what remained was useless. A later rabbinic story has Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah answer a question about how to salt salt that has lost its savor by asking whether a mule can bear young, since the thing is impossible (b. Bekhorot 8b). The verb in verse 34, mōrainō, means ‘to become foolish’ in Romans 1:22 and 1 Corinthians 1:20, and Luke's hearers may have caught the double sense: a disciple who loses his distinctiveness becomes both tasteless and foolish.
literary:
The chapter is set around one meal and moves in four steps, each triggered by what Jesus sees or hears: a healing with a question (1-6), advice to guests after he notices them choosing the best places (7-11), advice to the host (12-14), and a parable prompted by a guest's pious remark (15-24). Luke calls the advice to guests a parable (verse 7), which signals that it is more than etiquette: seating at a dinner is a picture of standing before God. The unit closes with a maxim that recurs in Luke, “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted” (verse 11; compare 1:52 and 18:14).

The parable of the banquet repeats the list from verse 13, the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, in verse 21, tying the host's table to the kingdom's. It has three excuses in rising order of finality (‘please excuse me’ twice, then ‘I cannot come’) and three movements of the servant: to the invited, into the city, and out to the roads. The guest's remark, “Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God” (verse 15), assumes that he and his fellow guests will be there; the parable answers that those who assume their place may refuse it, and those who assumed they had none will fill the house. The final line shifts from ‘you’ singular to ‘you’ plural (verse 24), so that the host of the parable speaks over the heads of the servant to everyone at the Pharisee's table.

The final section (25-35) is addressed to the crowds and has two paired parables of counting the cost, a builder and a king, one about a private project and one about a public war. They are framed by three statements that such a person ‘cannot be My disciple’ (verses 26, 27, 33), each naming a different claim that must yield: relationships, one's own life, and possessions. The pairing of an invitation that costs nothing to accept (15-24) with a call that costs everything (25-33) is deliberate. The salt saying closes with the call to hear that also ended the parable of the sower (8:8).

outline.t: A man with dropsy healed on the Sabbath
The parable of the great banquet
The cost of discipleship: tower and war

doctrines.note: The great banquet is God's invitation to his kingdom, prepared in full before anyone is called (“Come, for everything is now ready”, verse 17). The only way to miss it is to refuse. The kingdom reverses the world's order of honor: the humble are exalted, the self-promoting humbled, and the poor and disabled brought in first.

Jesus tells a host to invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind precisely because they cannot repay (verses 13-14). Generosity in the kingdom breaks the circle of social exchange and mirrors God's own hospitality in the parable that follows, where the same four groups fill the house (verse 21).

The reward for hospitality to those who cannot repay comes “at the resurrection of the righteous” (verse 14). Luke assumes a bodily resurrection and final judgment in which God himself repays what was given without return, a hope Paul also states before Felix (Acts 24:15).

Jesus requires a loyalty to himself above father, mother, wife, children, and siblings (verse 26). The idiom of hate means putting him first, not malice; the same Jesus upholds honoring parents (18:20). Family is a great good that becomes an idol when it competes with him, and following him may cost family approval.

The builder and the king count the cost before they begin (verses 28-32), and the section ends with the requirement to give up (apotassō, to say farewell to) everything one has (verse 33). Possessions, like family, cannot hold first place for a disciple, a theme Luke develops in the rich fool (12:13-21) and the rich ruler (18:18-30).

words.note: Tapeinoō, to make low, humble, humiliate. It occurs about 14 times in the New Testament, five of them in Luke. In verse 11 the passive ‘will be humbled’ is a divine passive: God is the one who brings the self-exalting low. The same maxim closes the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector (18:14), and Mary's song praises God who has exalted the humble (1:52, using the related adjective). Paul uses the verb of Christ, who humbled himself to death on a cross (Philippians 2:8).

Hupsoō, to lift up, exalt. It occurs about 20 times in the New Testament, six in Luke. In verse 11 it pairs with tapeinoō in a reversal that runs through Luke from the Magnificat (1:52) onward. In John the same verb describes the Son of Man ‘lifted up’ on the cross (John 3:14, 12:32), and in Acts 2:33 Christ is exalted to God's right hand: the humbled one is the exalted one.

Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up. It occurs about 42 times in the New Testament, six in Luke and eleven in Acts. The phrase ‘the resurrection of the righteous’ (verse 14) reflects Jewish hope for the raising of the dead at the end (Daniel 12:2). Luke uses the word again in the debate with the Sadducees (20:27-38) and makes the resurrection central to the apostles' preaching in Acts (4:2, 17:18).

Paraiteomai, to ask to be excused, decline, refuse. It occurs about 12 times in the New Testament, three of them in verses 18-19. The courteous form of the excuses, ‘please consider me excused’, masks a refusal. Hebrews 12:25 uses the same verb in its warning not to refuse the one who speaks from heaven, which is what the guests in the parable do.

Anagkazō, to compel, urge strongly, press. It occurs 9 times in the New Testament, and its range runs from force (Acts 26:11, where Paul tried to force believers to blaspheme) to strong persuasion (Matthew 14:22, where Jesus made the disciples get into the boat; Acts 16:15, where Lydia ‘persuaded’ Paul's company to stay, uses parabiazomai, a verb of similar force). In verse 23 a lone servant urges people on the roads who would never expect to be invited. Augustine's use of the word to justify state coercion of the Donatists is discussed below.

Miseō, to hate. It occurs about 40 times in the New Testament, seven in Luke. In ordinary Greek it means hostility, but in the Greek Old Testament it often renders the Hebrew sane', which can express rejection or lesser preference in a comparison (Genesis 29:31, Deuteronomy 21:15). In verse 26 it names a loyalty to Jesus so complete that every other claim, even one's own life, comes second. Luke also uses the word in its ordinary sense of enemies who hate the disciples (6:22, 6:27, 21:17).

Mathētēs, disciple, learner, apprentice. It occurs about 261 times in the New Testament, all in the Gospels and Acts, where it is the usual name for Jesus' followers (Acts 11:26). In verses 26, 27, and 33 the refrain ‘cannot be My disciple’ defines the word by its cost: a disciple is not a member of the crowd traveling with Jesus but one who follows him with everything.

Stauros, cross, the upright stake or crossbeam used for crucifixion. It occurs about 27 times in the New Testament. In verse 27 Jesus says a disciple must ‘carry’ (bastazō) his own cross, the verb John uses of Jesus carrying his (John 19:17). Luke's earlier form of the saying adds ‘daily’ (9:23), making the cross a pattern of life, but here, on the road to Jerusalem, it keeps its literal edge.

christ:
Jesus is both guest and host in this chapter. At the Pharisee's table he is watched closely (verse 1), and he watches in return (verse 7). He heals without being asked, takes hold of the man, and sends him on his way, and he exposes the scramble for honor that fills the room. In the parable the host who throws open his house to the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame is the God whom Jesus reveals, and the servant who goes out repeatedly with the invitation is a picture of Jesus' own mission, carried from the respectable to the streets and then to the roads beyond the town. Luke's readers would see the pattern continue in Acts, where the gospel goes first to Israel and then to the Gentiles.

He practices the humility he teaches. The one who took the lowest place will be exalted, a pattern Paul sees in Christ, who humbled himself to the point of death on a cross and was highly exalted (Philippians 2:8-9), and which Luke shows when Jesus tells his disciples at the Last Supper that he is among them as one who serves (22:27). His call to carry a cross and count the cost is spoken by one who has already counted it for himself, on the road to Jerusalem, where he will be the one who does not come down from the cross (23:35-39). The builder who finishes what he starts and the king who weighs the battle are images of the disciple, but they also fit Jesus, who set his face toward Jerusalem (9:51) and finished the work.

The chapter also shows who Jesus claims to be. He speaks of loyalty to himself as surpassing the claims of father and mother, which the Law ranked just after duty to God (Exodus 20:12). Only God could rightly ask that. The feast in the kingdom of God (verse 15) is one Jesus himself will host, as he promises at the Last Supper that his disciples will eat and drink at his table in his kingdom (22:29-30), and the resurrection of the righteous (verse 14) is guaranteed by his own resurrection, which Luke narrates at the end of his Gospel.
interpretation:
The banquet parable was read allegorically from early times. Gregory the Great preached on it in Rome in 591 (Homilies on the Gospels 36), contrasting bodily pleasures, which attract at first and then pall, with spiritual ones, which seem unattractive at first and grow sweeter with tasting, and reading the excuses as preoccupation with earthly property, curiosity, and the pleasures of the flesh. Many fathers took the first invited as Israel's leaders, the poor of the city as Israel's outcasts, and those on the highways as the Gentiles.

The command of verse 23 has the darkest history of any verse in the chapter. In North Africa the Donatists, a separatist church that had broken with the catholic bishops after the persecution under Diocletian, were suppressed by imperial law from 405. Augustine at first held that no one should be coerced into unity, only persuaded. In Letter 93 to Vincentius (around 408) he explained that he had changed his mind after seeing Donatists in his own city return under pressure of the imperial edicts and later thank God for it, and he cited compel them to come in as warrant for the church's appeal to state power. His Letter 185 to the tribune Boniface (around 417), later circulated as The Correction of the Donatists, developed the argument. Augustine urged restraint in penalties and opposed the death penalty for Donatists, but his reading became a standard proof text. Thomas Aquinas cited the verse when he argued that those who have never received the faith must not be compelled to believe, but that heretics and apostates may be compelled to keep what they once professed (Summa Theologiae II-II q.10 a.8). After Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685 and troops were quartered on Protestant households to force conversions, the Huguenot exile Pierre Bayle answered with his Philosophical Commentary on These Words of Jesus Christ, Compel Them to Come In (1686), arguing that a reading of Scripture that commands crimes must be false and that forced conversion is abominable. The Second Vatican Council's Declaration on Religious Freedom (Dignitatis Humanae, 1965) taught that no one may be forced to act against conscience in religious matters. Most modern commentators, Catholic and Protestant, read anagkazō here as urgent persuasion of people who would not believe the invitation was meant for them.

The saying about hating family has shaped Christian renunciation. Jerome's Letter 14 to Heliodorus (about 374) urged his friend to step over his own father on the threshold to take up the monastic life, a rhetorical extreme that later readers found troubling. Søren Kierkegaard, in Fear and Trembling (1843), refused to soften the word hate and made Luke 14:26 central to his account of an absolute duty to God that relativizes the ethical, with Abraham as his example. Dietrich Bonhoeffer's Discipleship (1937) opens its chapter on discipleship and the individual with this verse, arguing that Christ breaks every immediate tie so that all relationships, even to family, pass through him as mediator.

In Lutheran Leipzig the Gospel for the Second Sunday after Trinity was Luke 14:16-24, and Bach wrote Die Himmel erzählen die Ehre Gottes (BWV 76, 1723) and Ach Gott, vom Himmel sieh darein (BWV 2, 1724) for it; for the Seventeenth Sunday after Trinity, when Luke 14:1-11 was read, he wrote Wer sich selbst erhöhet, der soll erniedriget werden (BWV 47, 1726), whose title is verse 11. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year C, 14:1 and 7-14 are read in late August or early September (Proper 17) and 14:25-33 the following week (Proper 18); the Roman lectionary reads the same passages on the Twenty-second and Twenty-third Sundays in Ordinary Time in Year C.
text:
Verse 5 has a significant variant. The earliest papyri, P45 and P75, with Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Vaticanus, and most later manuscripts, read ‘a son or an ox’ (huios ē bous). Codex Sinaiticus and a number of other witnesses read ‘a donkey or an ox’ (onos ē bous), which the Textus Receptus and the King James Version follow (‘an ass or an ox’); a few manuscripts have ‘a sheep or an ox’. In the abbreviated Greek of early manuscripts the words for son and donkey looked alike. The familiar pairing of ox and donkey (Deuteronomy 22:4, Luke 13:15) would tempt a copyist to change ‘son’ to ‘donkey’, while there was no reason to change it the other way, so most editors accept ‘son’. The reading makes Jesus' argument sharper: no one would leave his own child in a well on the Sabbath.

In verse 3 the earliest manuscripts include the words ‘or not’ (ē ou) after the question whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, which later copies omit. In verse 21 later manuscripts reverse the order of the lame and the blind. These do not change the meaning.

teach.big: God's kingdom is a feast freely prepared for those who cannot repay, entered by the humble who accept the invitation, and it claims first place over every other love, possession, and plan.

outline.t: Jesus heals in the face of hostile scrutiny; mercy on the Sabbath is what everyone already practices for their own.
Honor is God's to give; those who grasp for status before him will be humbled, and those who take the low place will be lifted.
Kingdom hospitality gives to those who cannot repay and trusts God to repay at the resurrection.
The kingdom is ready and the invitation is urgent; ordinary goods become excuses, and the house fills with those who never expected to be asked.
Following Jesus costs everything: loyalty above family, one's own life, and possessions; count the cost before you begin.
A disciple who loses the distinctive mark of discipleship is as useless as salt without taste; hear and heed.

teach.pitfalls:
The advice about seats (7-11) is often preached as a clever tactic for getting honored in the end, which inverts it. Jesus calls it a parable, and its point is humility before God, who alone exalts. Taking the low seat in order to be moved up is simply a subtler way of seeking honor. The advice to hosts (12-14) is sometimes dismissed as hyperbole or spiritualized into generosity of heart; Luke means real meals and real guests, and Acts shows the early church sharing tables across social lines (Acts 2:46, 6:1).

The banquet parable should not be read as teaching that God's invitation depends on social status in reverse, as if poverty itself saved; the poor come because they accept, and the invited are shut out because they refuse. Verse 23 must never be preached as warrant for pressure, manipulation, or coercion in evangelism; its history of misuse, from the Donatist controversy to the dragonnades, is a warning. With verse 26, avoid two opposite errors: softening hate into something that costs nothing, and using the verse to justify abandoning or despising family, which the rest of Scripture forbids (18:20, Mark 7:9-13, 1 Timothy 5:8). The cost-counting parables are not a call to delay commitment until one is sure one can pay; they warn against a casual following that has not reckoned with the cross.
teach.pastoral: Verse 26 will press on people whose faith has cost them family: converts disowned by parents, spouses whose partner resents their faith, and adult children estranged over religion. Honor that cost without making estrangement a badge. It will also be heard by people with harsh or abusive family histories, who may take it as permission for bitterness, and by those who fear it demands that they abandon a spouse or children; say plainly that Jesus asks for first place, not for cruelty, and that caring for one's household is itself a duty to him. The banquet's list of guests speaks to people with disabilities, who are too often left out of church life, and to all who feel they have nothing to offer God. Verse 23 may reopen wounds for those pressured into religious commitment; they deserve to hear that Jesus' invitation compels by grace, not by force.

hard.q: How can Jesus tell his followers to hate their families?
hard.a:
Few sayings sound harsher, and critics have used it to charge Jesus with teaching the destruction of families; some groups have used it to justify cutting members off from their relatives. Søren Kierkegaard, who was no critic of Christianity, insisted in Fear and Trembling (1843) that the word must not be softened, since softening it turns something terrible into a mild platitude. The Gospel of Thomas preserves the saying in stark form twice (sayings 55 and 101), once alongside a saying that the disciple must also love father and mother as Jesus does, which shows that early readers already felt its tension.

The main responses read the word in its biblical idiom without draining it of force. In Hebrew usage to love one and hate another often means to choose one over the other (Genesis 29:30-31, Deuteronomy 21:15-17, Malachi 1:2-3), and Matthew's parallel says whoever loves father or mother more than Jesus is not worthy of him (Matthew 10:37). The same Jesus insists on honoring father and mother (18:20), condemns those who evade support for their parents (Mark 7:9-13), and provides for his mother from the cross (John 19:26-27). Still, the idiom should not be softened into nothing. In the first century following Jesus could mean being cast out by family (12:51-53), as it still does for many believers, and Jesus wants would-be followers to know that loyalty to him may cost the closest relationships. The list ends with ‘even his own life’, which shows that the point is not animosity toward others but the surrender of every competing claim, including self-love. Dietrich Bonhoeffer (Discipleship, 1937) argued that Christ stands between the disciple and every other person, so that family is loved through him and not apart from him. On this reading the saying relativizes family rather than rejecting it, and it makes a claim only God could rightly make, which is part of what Luke wants his readers to notice about Jesus.

hard.q: Does “compel them to come in” justify forcing people into the faith?
hard.a:
Augustine thought it could justify pressure. In Letter 93 (around 408) and Letter 185 (around 417) he argued that the church could rightly welcome imperial laws against the Donatists, since many who were driven back into catholic unity later embraced it gladly, and he read the servant's compelling in verse 23 as the church's warrant for calling on the state. He distinguished corrective pressure from cruelty and opposed executing Donatists, and he argued that the church acts from love, as a father disciplines a son. Thomas Aquinas cited the verse when he taught that heretics and apostates may be compelled to keep the faith they once professed (Summa Theologiae II-II q.10 a.8). The argument had real force in its setting: the Donatist conflict had involved violence on both sides, including attacks by the Circumcellions on catholic clergy, and the state already enforced religious law.

The responses are historical, textual, and theological. Historically, the verse became a license for persecution, and its use to justify the forced conversions of French Protestants after 1685 prompted Pierre Bayle's Philosophical Commentary (1686), which argued that any literal reading of Scripture that commands injustice must be mistaken and that coerced belief is no belief. Textually, anagkazō ranges from force to earnest urging, and in the parable a single servant speaks to people on the roads who would never believe that a rich man's feast was meant for them; the natural sense is insistent persuasion, as when the Emmaus disciples ‘urged’ Jesus to stay (24:29, using parabiazomai, a verb of similar force). Theologically, the parable's host has no power over the guests who refuse, and Jesus himself never coerced belief, rebuking disciples who wanted to call down fire on an unwelcoming Samaritan village (9:52-55). The Roman Catholic Church's Declaration on Religious Freedom (1965) and the historic Baptist and Anabaptist witness for liberty of conscience both reject coercion in religion, and modern commentators across traditions read the verse as urgency, not force.

observe: What four groups does Jesus tell the host to invite in verse 13, and where do the same groups appear again in the chapter?
What three excuses do the invited guests give, and how does each one differ from the others?
What three things does Jesus say a person must do or give up, or else they ‘cannot be My disciple’ (verses 26, 27, 33)?
interpret: Why does Luke call Jesus' advice about seats a ‘parable’ (verse 7)? What is it really about?
How does the guest's remark in verse 15 set up the parable of the banquet? Who is the parable aimed at?
How should the word hate in verse 26 be understood, and what would be lost if it were softened too far?
apply: Think of a gathering you will host or attend soon. What would it look like to apply Jesus' advice about seats and invitations?
The invited guests had reasonable-sounding excuses: property, work, and marriage. What good things tend to become excuses for you?
Jesus urges would-be followers to count the cost. What has following Jesus cost you, and what might it cost in the future?
